How would hacking be without knowledge, skills or creativity? 

The same "hacks" get applied repetitively to open ports and then read/download/delete files over and over again. I've seen more challenging escape rooms.

Don't get me wrong - It's amazing for an indie game developed by one person. But on the other hand there are CTFs with a nice story out there that keep me busy without making me feel like in a hamster wheel. If you are into cyber security, don't waste your time with this. 

But if you have zero knowledge and want to feel like a hacker, this game teaches a few basics about handling a Linux-like OS (with wine for .exe files) and simulates how to move through a network.

It would be great to focus on only a few stories and individualize the targets instead of seeing generic ancient bash content on every PC. Also I missed a proper C2 setup with own proxies that I can create, privilege escalation and lateral movement instead of being admin immediately, alternating attack vectors and the option to create scripts or at least files ("touch") and directories ("mkdir"). This would have been a nice starting point to start playing around, break things out of curiosity and discover the possibilities instead of moving inside the box all the time.

Hacknet is an absolutely INCREDIBLE game in nearly every aspect, and here's my opinion on everything about it.

(But first, one quick thing: Before it meant... well, its current definition, "gay" was defined as "happy or joyful," such as how it is used in many classic Christmas carols. BY THAT DEFINITION ONLY, this game has made me gay. Read on for more.)

First, a bit of info on Hacknet. It is an immersive, Unix-based terminal hacking simulator that has you investigating the death of a hacker known as Bit. But first, Bit's pre-recorded emails will tell you everything you need to know about hacking. So, yeah. It takes about 4-5 hours to beat, so it's a really good way to spend an afternoon.

The story is absolutely INCREDIBLE: it is so carefully written to be as compelling as possible. It teaches you how to play without distracting you from the story, saving the toughest bits for last... which brings us into the gameplay. Hacknet is designed so that you have to consider every possible angle before you can solve it. Need a password? Scan the network and see what you find. Can't break a port? Check other servers - your faction's assets server may be helpful, as will other servers on the network you're breaking. It keeps you trying and trying until you finally solve it, and then you feel accomplished. It's pretty dang good.

I have one MAJOR gripe with Hacknet, though: the Unix accuracy. It claims to be a Unix-based hacking simulator, and then proceeds to slap Windows files - .exe, .bat, .msi, and so forth - on EVERY SINGLE SERVER IN THE GAME. Like, what the heck?!?

Other than that, though, I'm amazed you read through this whole review. I mean, the buy button is at the top of the webpage.

I got this game for not even 1,50 euros, but I'll still be reviewing it as its full price (since it's not like everyone will buy it on sale).

For just about 10 bucks, this game gives you an incredible experience. An engaging storyline, interesting puzzles/detective work, some funny moments, and... a clicker mini-game?

Visually, this game is very nice too! The funky little animations gave me enough dopamine to push through the pain my tiny technologically-illiterate brain was going through as I struggled to understand any of the game's terminology. Being able to change the UI's theme is also very nice (even though I found myself rarely ever changing it).

Music-wise, the soundtrack is decently good. Nothing outstanding enough to stick with me, but enough to make me bob my head from time to time.

My favourite thing, though, is how important NOTE TAKING IS! Genuinely, this is one of the best things in games, and I feel like I rarely see it! Throughout the game you'll have to take notes on different passwords and IPs to check out later, which really makes you feel like you're actually digging through stuff, enhancing the immersion into the hacking fantasy.

For it's price, you can very easily get your money's worth in game time, specially if you like to explore all the files with flavor text and go out achievement hunting.

Also, just one final thing. I was NOT expecting to feel mortified at seeing some numbers go high and then go down to zero, but here we are.

If you've ever tried to learn to navigate a computer or network via the terminal, and enjoyed it when you got it to do what you wanted it to do, then you'll probably like HackNet. It's gamified hacking, with a really comfortable learning curve. It does expect you to learn the game's command-script language, but it's simplified and very accessible, as well as rewarding should you take the time to learn how to use it to its fullest. The story and dialogue are engaging and well-paced, and there's plenty of entertaining chat logs to browse while you're digging around on other peoples' computers. Not to mention, the soundtrack is absolute fire.

So far HackNet has provided me with some healthy doses of adrenaline, and the perfect amount of challenge; enough to keep my brain engaged with whatever puzzle I'm solving, without driving me to the point of frustration. I'm well immersed, and for the price, it's a steal. Highly recommend.

This is one of the best games I've ever played and I recommend it to anyone relatively familiar with computers, especially anyone who's dabbled in Linux, command lines, or coding. Even if the extent of your experience is just installing mods for games or messing around with file trees.

Here's the deal. It's obviously not real hacking. It will not teach you how to hack irl, which is probably a good thing. However, it does a good job at capturing the feeling of having years of experience hacking and being able to do it relatively effortlessly.

The interface is a moderate challenge to figure out, but it's very important that the learning curve is there. You actually need to learn a little bit of the command structures and how to run your hacking programs. Once you complete your first several hacks, most of the hacking itself becomes second nature. You know exactly how to break into basically anything. This is where the game really takes off in my opinion.

Sure you can break into anything, but are you being paranoid about leaving no trace behind? Can you do it fast enough to not get caught? Can you figure out exactly what you need to do once you've broken in? You can't just break into computers and expect that everything will turn out alright. Once you get deeper into the game, the risk of being caught or counter-hacked becomes exponentially bigger as your targets become more and more advanced. You will need to restore your own files somehow. You will need to have a few defenses in place for when you're inevitably attacked. And the game will not necessarily teach you how to do that. You'll have to think on your feet and be creative with solutions. Often there are multiple solutions that will work, and they potentially have different outcomes.

This game does not hold your hand and it is all the better for it. If you need help, you can find it, sure. But the game won't give you anything for free. Figuring out how to use the tools at your disposal is part of the learning process and it's far better for it. Within 2 hours you'll feel like an amateur script kitty hacker that's untouchable, but by the 3rd and 4th hour you'll be humbled by how vulnerable you really are.

Overall it's a really fun and unique experience that imo would be worth the full asking price. However, it goes on sale every few months for like $1.49. At that price it's an absolute steal and worth every penny. If you're even remotely interested in hacking and computers, pick it up sometime.
